title: 1 Kings 7:40–51
context: This unit summarizes Hiram’s bronze work (7:40–47) and then lists the gold furnishings Solomon made for the inside of the house (7:48–50), before closing the building account with the deposit of David’s dedicated things in the treasuries (7:51). The bronze was cast in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan (7:46), and there was so much that it was never weighed (7:47); 1 Chronicles 18:8 says the bronze for the sea, the pillars, and the vessels came from cities of Hadadezer that David conquered. Parallel differences, stated without harmonization: 2 Chronicles 4:17 names the casting site as between Succoth and Zeredah; 1 Kings 7:48 speaks of the table for the show bread in the singular, while 2 Chronicles 4:8 says Solomon made ten tables and 2 Chronicles 4:19 speaks of the tables with the show bread on them. Chapter 8 follows with the ark brought in and the cloud of the LORD’s glory filling the house (8:10–11). Both traditions read this unit as the completion of the building account and as shared ground: the house is finished, and its meaning will depend on the LORD’s presence and Israel’s covenant faithfulness (6:12–13).

verses.text: Hiram made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished doing all the work that he worked for King Solomon in the LORD’s house:
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram makes the pots, shovels, and basins and finishes all his work for King Solomon in the LORD’s house. Arminian readers note the faithful completion of a large, demanding commission. A skilled worker from Tyre carries his task through to the end, and the narrator honors his labor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completion as part of God’s faithfulness in bringing the promised house to completion (2 Samuel 7:13), working through human means. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking the end of Hiram’s work and affirm that God is honored through faithful, skilled labor.

verses.text: the two pillars; the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars; the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars;
verses.arminianNotes: The summary list begins with the two pillars, their capitals, and their networks. Arminian readers see the narrator recapping the major bronze works so that the reader can take in the whole. The repetition serves as a record of completion rather than introducing new details or meanings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the inventory as the narrator’s formal summary of Hiram’s work. Lists like this function as records, much like the tabernacle inventories in Exodus. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recapitulation and agree that it raises no theological difference.

verses.text: the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks; two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;
verses.arminianNotes: The four hundred pomegranates for the two networks are listed. Arminian readers note that the total matches 2 Chronicles 4:13, while the earlier count in 7:20 and the figure in 2 Chronicles 3:16 differ, as the context records. They see no need to resolve these figures by speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the verse as part of the summary inventory. They acknowledge the parallel figures plainly and affirm the record’s trustworthiness without forcing harmony. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recapping the decoration of the capitals and decline to build doctrine on the count.

verses.text: the ten bases; the ten basins on the bases;
verses.arminianNotes: The ten bases and ten basins are listed. Arminian readers see the inventory continuing in orderly fashion. The verse adds nothing new to the description in 7:27–39 but confirms that the work was completed as planned, which the narrator treats as worth recording.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the verse as part of the formal list. The narrator’s orderly summary reflects the careful completion of the LORD’s house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an inventory line that confirms completion and raises no point of disagreement between them.

verses.text: the one sea; the twelve oxen under the sea;
verses.arminianNotes: The one sea with the twelve oxen under it is listed. Arminian readers note the brevity of the summary after the fuller description in 7:23–26. The inventory reminds the reader of the scale of Hiram’s achievement without adding interpretation or symbolism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the line as recapitulation. They note that the same items appear again in the account of their destruction by the Chaldeans (2 Kings 25:13, 16). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the inventory, and both see in later history the impermanence of even the finest temple furnishings.

verses.text: the pots; the shovels; and the basins. All of these vessels, which Hiram made for King Solomon for the LORD’s house, were of burnished bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: The pots, shovels, and basins complete the list, all of burnished bronze, made by Hiram for King Solomon for the LORD’s house. Arminian readers note the dignity given to humble utensils. Every item, however ordinary, was made with care for the worship of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note that even ordinary utensils were made of burnished bronze for the LORD’s house. They see this as fitting honor for the place where God chose to put his name. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming that the whole of the work, small and great, was offered for the LORD’s service.

verses.text: The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.
verses.arminianNotes: The king casts the bronze in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan. Arminian readers note the practical choice of a suitable site for large castings. The precise location, which 2 Chronicles 4:17 names with Zeredah, is recorded in the context without speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as a historical note about where the casting took place. The narrator anchors the account in real geography. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as factual detail, note the parallel name honestly, and see no theological question raised by the location.

verses.text: Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them. The weight of the bronze could not be determined.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon leaves the bronze vessels unweighed because there were so many. Arminian readers see the abundance of the kingdom’s resources, gained in part through David’s victories (1 Chronicles 18:8). The verse emphasizes the generosity and scale of what was devoted to the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same abundance as a sign of God’s blessing on David and Solomon, supplying more than could be measured. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing lavish provision for the LORD’s house, and both note that the bronze was again left unweighed when it was carried away (2 Kings 25:16).

verses.text: Solomon made all the vessels that were in the LORD’s house: the golden altar and the table that the show bread was on, of gold;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes the gold vessels for the LORD’s house: the golden altar and the table for the show bread. Arminian readers note the continuity with the tabernacle furnishings (Exodus 25:23–30). Israel’s worship continues in a new, permanent setting, still shaped by what God had commanded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity between the tabernacle and the temple furnishings, both shaped by God’s instructions. 2 Chronicles 4:8 and 4:19 speak of tables, a difference recorded in the context. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing worship ordered by God and decline to allegorize the furnishings.

verses.text: and the lamp stands, five on the right side and five on the left, in front of the inner sanctuary, of pure gold; and the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;
verses.arminianNotes: Ten lamp stands of pure gold stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side, with flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold. Arminian readers note the expansion from the tabernacle’s single lamp stand (Exodus 25:31) to ten, reflecting the larger house and the greater resources of Solomon’s day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the continuity with the tabernacle lamp stand and its expansion in the temple. Shared ground: both traditions read the lamp stands as part of the ordered worship of the LORD’s house; both note that the parallel at 2 Chronicles 4:7 likewise speaks of ten lamp stands, and neither assigns a separate symbolic meaning to their number.

verses.text: the cups, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and the fire pans, of pure gold; and the hinges, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, of the temple, of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Cups, snuffers, basins, spoons, fire pans, and the door hinges are all of gold. Arminian readers note the thoroughness of the work, down to the hinges of the doors of the most holy place. Nothing used in the LORD’s house was treated as too small for care and honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the gold extending to the smallest items as fitting honor for the place of God’s presence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the richness and completeness of the furnishings, and both affirm that the worship of God deserves wholehearted devotion without reading allegory into the hinges.

verses.text: Thus all the work that King Solomon did in the LORD’s house was finished. Solomon brought in the things which David his father had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and the vessels—and put them in the treasuries of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The work is finished, and Solomon places David’s dedicated silver, gold, and vessels in the treasuries (compare 2 Samuel 8:11). Arminian readers note that the house is complete, but its meaning still depends on covenant faithfulness (6:12–13), as the coming dedication will stress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completed house as the fulfillment of God’s promise that David’s son would build a house for his name (2 Samuel 7:13), with David’s gifts carried into it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the building account and as preparing for the LORD’s glory to fill the house (8:10–11).
